chapter: New York 1948: Tristano and the Miles nonet
title: Holman's 'A Personal Voice' and playing sharp
summary: He relates his sharp pitch to the Holman piece written for him, and tells a Jackie McLean story at the Vanguard.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Reeds, mouthpieces and horns: the reed player's gear

blocks.x: But this record that I gave you, I think you’re getting a “five minute notice” . . . oh, I shouldn’t have said that [chuckles]. [Konitz takes a moment to remember what he had been referring to]
The record I gave you of Holman…

With the Metropole Orchestra. Oh, the piece that he wrote for me he called “A Personal Voice” and the fact is, I think, that’s part of the character of my sound: up on the line of the pitch, or over sometimes. I lived with that positively and negatively over the years, but that’s it. When I sat at the Village Vanguard one time at the bar, Cedar Walton played as a trio and then called Jackie McLean up. Larry Willis was sitting in front of me at the bar and Jackie was really sharp.
Larry turned around and said: “He can push it in or pull it out but don’t leave it were it is”.
Then I went back stage after the set and I said: “I meant to talk to you about this”. He didn’t want to hear about it. That was it.
He and Charlie Rouse were the ultimate sharp saxophone players.
Uh-huh, Charlie Rouse. Bird was pretty sharp at the beginning, and Sonny Rollins.
